clips.text_en_b1: Spoiler alert. Pumptober! BTC broke ATH. BULL RUN CONFIRMED. Crypto will finally pump. It will pump for Christmas. Then Chinese New Year. Then when capital rotates out of AI. Then out of gold. Then when DUMP announces something at WEF. Then when the Clarity Act passes. Loop this five times. We did not need yet another pump-delay cope thread for fall 2026.

signal.rationale: Implied long bias from pump cope, but multiple delays and zero new catalyst erode conviction

clips.text_en_b2: Pumptober spoiler incoming. Bitcoin has shattered its all-time high, so naturally everyone is calling for a bullish run. Crypto will pump by Christmas, then again around Chinese New Year, then once capital rotates out of AI, then again when gold loses its shine. Meanwhile we are still waiting for the Clarity Act to pass and for some vague DUMP announcement at the WEF summit. Loop that five times. Honestly, we did not need another pump-delay cope thread for fall 2026.
clips.text_en_c1: A heads-up for anyone who has been waiting on the next leg up. Pumptober is supposedly upon us: BTC decisively breached its all-time high, and the prevailing consensus is that the long-anticipated bull run has at last commenced. By all accounts, the rally should materialise in time for Christmas, then continue through Chinese New Year, then resume whenever money rotates out of AI equities and subsequently out of gold. Thereafter it will ostensibly await a pronouncement from DUMP at the World Economic Forum, and finally crystallise once the Clarity Act is passed. Loop that sequence five times. Frankly, we did not require yet another pump-delay cope thread for autumn 2026.
clips.text_en_c2: Spoiler alert: Pumptober has ostensibly arrived. Bitcoin breached its all-time high, the prevailing narrative insists, and the long-anticipated crypto rally has, by all accounts, been confirmed. Yet the pump remains stubbornly postponed, deferred ad infinitum until the Clarity Act passes, until DUMP deigns to make an announcement at Davos, until capital finally rotates out of artificial intelligence equities and out of gold. Loop this catechism five times, preferably with the fervour of true believers, and you might persuade yourself that Christmas, the Lunar New Year, or some equally arbitrary milestone will deliver the breakout we have been promised. Alas, fall 2026 has produced yet another pump-delay cope thread, indistinguishable in spirit from its predecessors, save that the season has changed.

clips.text_en_b1: Which stocks should I buy? I'm leaning towards SpaceX but I'm open to ideas. Serious answers only. Pre-IPO shares trade on secondary markets, but minimums are huge and lockup risk is real for retail. Bought SPY puts last month, currently deciding if I sell for a loss or hold through earnings. signal.rationale: No actionable setup, just a pick request

clips.text_en_b2: Looking for solid stock picks, leaning heavily towards SpaceX but open to suggestions. Pre-IPO shares do exist on secondary markets, although the minimum lot sizes are frankly absurd and the lockup risk is genuinely concerning for retail investors. I picked up some SPY puts last month, and right now I am weighing up whether to cut my losses before earnings or hold out and hope for a turnaround. Any serious advice would be appreciated. Not financial advice, obviously.
clips.text_en_c1: I find myself inclined towards acquiring a position in SpaceX, although I remain genuinely receptive to alternative suggestions, provided the responses are substantive rather than facetious. Pre-IPO shares are technically available on secondary markets, yet the minimum ticket sizes tend to be prohibitively large for retail participants, and the lockup risk is a genuine concern, should one ever wish to exit. I purchased SPY puts last month and currently face the unenviable decision of crystallising the loss or holding through the forthcoming earnings cycle. Not financial advice, naturally. Has anyone actually navigated the pre-IPO landscape successfully?
clips.text_en_c2: I find myself gravitating toward SpaceX as a prospective position, though I remain genuinely receptive to alternative suggestions; substantive counsel would be most welcome. The principal obstacle, as any retail investor would recognise, is that SpaceX has yet to undertake an initial public offering, and the secondary markets on which pre-IPO shares occasionally trade impose prohibitively substantial minimums alongside a lockup risk that renders the proposition rather unpalatable. Prop firm allocations, similarly, are grotesquely insufficient to be of practical use. Meanwhile, I initiated a position in SPY puts last month and presently find myself deliberating whether to crystallise the loss ahead of earnings or to persist in holding the position through the imminent print. This constitutes observation, not financial advice.

clips.text_zh: 今日返工同Tommy傾beam design 連續梁係statically indeterminate 要用three-moment equation或者moment distribution method解 我個FE考牌書mark到花晒 🧐 load path記到 但release moment就亂
clips.text_en_b1: How do you decide which method to use for a continuous beam? Today at work we had a four-span continuous beam with UDL and two point loads, and the senior wanted moment distribution because it's easier to check by hand. I'm studying moment distribution and three-moment equation for the FE, but I keep mixing up the carry-over factors and stiffness coefficients.
clips.source_hint: /g/ thread about choosing the right structural analysis method

signal.rationale: FE study topic, not a trade

clips.text_en_b2: At work today I was discussing a four-span continuous beam with Tommy, loaded with a UDL and two point loads. The senior engineer insisted on moment distribution since it is far easier to cross-check by hand. I am currently grinding through both moment distribution and the three-moment equation for my FE exam, although I keep mixing up the carry-over factors and stiffness coefficients. Both methods yield identical results, so which approach do practising engineers genuinely favour on site?
clips.text_en_c1: What criteria do you typically apply when selecting an analytical method for a continuous beam? At the office today we were presented with a four-span continuous beam subject to a uniformly distributed load and two superimposed point loads, and the senior engineer insisted upon moment distribution on the grounds that it lends itself more readily to manual verification. For the Fundamentals of Engineering examination I am diligently revising both moment distribution and the three-moment equation, yet I find myself persistently conflating carry-over factors with stiffness coefficients. Although both techniques ultimately converge on identical results, which would you realistically deploy in practice on site?
clips.text_en_c2: How ought one to adjudicate between competing analytical methodologies when confronted with a statically indeterminate continuous beam? Earlier today a colleague and I were reviewing a four-span configuration subjected to a uniformly distributed load and two concentrated point loads, whereupon the senior engineer insisted upon moment distribution on the grounds that hand verification is appreciably more tractable than its alternatives. I am presently revising both moment distribution and the three-moment equation in preparation for the Fundamentals of Engineering examination, yet I find myself persistently conflating the relevant stiffness coefficients with their corresponding carry-over factors, a confusion that proves rather vexing at every iteration. Both approaches yield identical results in theory, of course, but which method does the practising engineer actually deploy on site?

clips.text_zh: Anthropic講AI R&D 270日就全自動 屌⋯⋯咁我仲讀咩FE呀？十年後civil engineer都係得2-4% neuron未明 😂 算 至少我手寫嘅beam check AI學唔到先⋯⋯應該
clips.text_en_b1: Anthropic believes AI R&D will become fully automated in about 270 days. You should spend every one of those 270 days doing something meaningful, because there is a decent chance you only get that amount of time. Make every meal count. Visit your parents. Read the books you always planned to read.
clips.source_hint: /g/ thread about Anthropic claim that AI R&D will be automated in 270 days
clips.text_en_b2: Anthropic is claiming that fully automated AI research and development is roughly 270 days away, so I am having a quiet existential crisis about my FE studies. Apparently only 2 to 4 percent of what a civil engineer does involves neural pathways nobody has fully mapped, which is not exactly comforting. On the bright side, my hand-written beam checks should be beyond AI's reach, or at least that is what I am choosing to believe for now.
clips.text_en_c1: Anthropic has publicly stated its conviction that artificial intelligence research and development will achieve full automation within approximately 270 days, which raises the rather uncomfortable question of what one ought to be doing with one's time in the interim. Should the prediction prove accurate, roughly 2-4% of neurons in the human brain remain functionally uncharacterised, a statistic that offers cold comfort to practising civil engineers. On a marginally more reassuring front, the bespoke hand calculations I perform for beam checks may yet prove resistant to algorithmic replication, though admittedly I would not stake my professional reputation on that assumption holding indefinitely.
clips.text_en_c2: Anthropic has, with characteristic audacity, posited that fully autonomous artificial intelligence research and development lies approximately two hundred and seventy days hence — a forecast that, if borne out, would render the remainder of my civil engineering licensure preparation rather academic. Within a decade, structural engineers may constitute but a marginal fraction of the cognitively unmodelled workforce, that scant two to four per cent whose neurons remain stubbornly inscrutable to the prevailing architectures. Be that as it may, I console myself with the hypothesis that the artisanal rigour of hand-executed beam checks — the meticulous notation, the laborious arithmetic — represents a craft beyond the machine’s present capacity. I daresay the assumption may prove optimistic.

clips.text_zh: BYD $9700 entry-level 400km 30分鐘充80% 仲要puncture-safe 同Tesla一樣tech 但係⋯⋯平過部iPhone多幾倍 🇺🇸 美國飛天車fail 因為I-curve搞唔掂啦 廢物
clips.text_en_b1: China BYD: $9700 retail. 400km range, charges 80% in 30 minutes, puncture-safe battery, all the trim and tech of a Tesla. U.S. flying cars fail. Cheap Chinese EVs are entering the market with decent specs, and US makers are distracted by gimmicks. Real talk: a $9,700 BYD undercuts every used Tesla and most new Honda Civics on price alone.
clips.source_hint: /pol/ thread hyping BYD's $9700 retail price against US automakers

signal.rationale: News thread, no direct trade setup

clips.text_en_b2: China's BYD now sells for a staggering $9,700 retail, offering a 400-kilometre range, an 80 percent charge in just 30 minutes, and puncture-safe batteries to boot, essentially matching Tesla's trim and technology at a fraction of the price. Meanwhile American flying car projects keep failing because nobody can sort out the impossible I-curve dynamics. At that price point, a BYD undercuts practically every used Tesla on the market, and most new Honda Civics too.
clips.text_en_c1: The entry-level BYD is presently retailing at approximately $9,700, a figure that warrants serious consideration. The vehicle delivers a 400-kilometre range, replenishes 80% of its battery within half an hour, and incorporates puncture-resistant cell technology, all while offering the trim and technological sophistication one would expect from a contemporary Tesla. American flying-car ventures, by contrast, have floundered, having failed to negotiate the notoriously unforgiving I-curve. Whether one views this as amusing or merely emblematic of misplaced priorities is a matter of personal disposition. Stripped of any rhetorical flourishes, a sub-ten-thousand-dollar BYD undercuts virtually every used Tesla and a substantial proportion of new economy cars purely on price.
clips.text_en_c2: Consider, if you will, the chasm in industrial philosophy between two great powers. The Chinese automaker BYD now retails an electric vehicle at the scarcely believable figure of nine thousand seven hundred dollars, a sum conferring four hundred kilometres of operational range, an eighty per cent charge achievable within the half-hour, and a puncture-resistant battery architecture — all whilst furnishing the technological refinements one might reasonably associate with a Tesla. Meanwhile, in the United States, the much-vaunted flying car remains perennially beset by the practical exigencies of the I-curve, a problem its engineers appear incapable of resolving. American manufacturers, distracted by gimmickry and grandiose spectacle, have ceded the substantive market to Chinese EVs whose specifications are eminently respectable and whose pricing undercuts every used Tesla and most contemporary Honda Civics.

clips.text_zh: 2.5年 275跌到179 仍然no gf 😢 同事對我好咗 但⋯⋯可能只係新工grind 廢物 我健身係為咗自己 ok 但有時⋯⋯肥仔信今日又chicken leg我 知唔知呀屌 lol
clips.text_en_b1: Lost 100 lbs, still no gf. Never had a gf and used to be fat as fuck at 275 lbs. Started going to the gym because my sister made her husband take me. He told me lose the weight and you'll find a gf fast. 2.5 years later I'm 179 lbs and look pretty fit, but still no gf.
clips.source_hint: /fit/ thread about weight loss without romance payoff
clips.text_en_b2: Dropped from 275 to 179 pounds over two and a half years, yet I still do not have a girlfriend. I never had one to begin with, and back then I was absolutely enormous. My sister eventually forced her husband to drag me to the gym, and he confidently told me that shedding the weight would have girls lining up. Fast forward to today, I look reasonably fit, but my bench is still nothing.
clips.text_en_c1: Over the course of two and a half years I have shed approximately 100 pounds, descending from a peak of 275 to a considerably more presentable 179, and yet I remain, much to my quiet frustration, without a girlfriend. My sister, exasperated by my circumstances, prevailed upon her husband to escort me to the gym, whereupon he offered the now rather dubious assurance that shedding the weight would swiftly resolve my romantic predicament. Colleagues at my new workplace have demonstrably warmed towards me, although I harbour lingering suspicions that this may simply reflect the honeymoon period of a fresh professional environment.
clips.text_en_c2: I shed a hundred pounds over the course of two and a half years, descending from a frankly corpulent two hundred and seventy-five to a comparatively svelte one hundred and seventy-nine, and I find myself, somewhat to my disquiet, still without a girlfriend. I had never enjoyed such a relationship, having previously subsisted in the unlovely condition of severe obesity, until my sibling prevailed upon her husband to escort me to the gym. He offered the somewhat reductive counsel that, were I to lose the weight, romantic success would swiftly materialise — a prophecy that, two and a half years hence, remains conspicuously unfulfilled. Female colleagues at my new employment are, I confess, marginally more solicitous, though one suspects the novelty of the workplace accounts for this. Chicken legs again today, incidentally.

clips.text_en_c1: A fresh storytime covering Ranma 1/2 is being run concurrently with the newly released anime adaptation, thereby affording viewers the rather enviable luxury of comparing and contrasting the two interpretations, or simply savouring the narrative through multiple lenses. Today's instalment encompasses chapters 53 through 55, in which Akane finally loses patience with Ranma in front of the entire class, and Happosai, in his inimitable fashion, absconds with the engagement photograph. The recent Netflix remake has, somewhat controversially, excised the cursed spring lore altogether, so the original manga serves as an indispensable reference for understanding precisely why cold water has such an unfortunate transformative effect upon the protagonist.
clips.text_en_c2: A long-overdue storytime of Takahashi Rumiko’s magnum opus, Ranma ½, is presently being conducted in parallel with the release of Netflix’s reimagined adaptation, thereby affording anon the rare privilege of comparing and contrasting the source material with its contemporary interpretation, or of experiencing the narrative through complementary aesthetic registers. Today’s instalment encompasses chapters fifty-three through fifty-five, in which Akane at last explodes at Ranma before the assembled gaze of the entire class, and Happosai absconds with the engagement photograph with characteristic alacrity. The remake, regrettably, has excised much of the cursed spring mythology, a lapse the original manga redresses with aplomb, explaining why mere cold water transforms our hapless protagonist into his feminine alter ego.
